Oxygen consumption was measured with a Clark electrode at 25 °C in the presence of ADP. Each inhibitor or uncoupler was added at a saturating concentration, and succinate was added where noted. Table 1 gives oxygen consumption in nmol of O2 per minute per mg of protein.
table_data:
| Condition | Oxygen consumption |
|---|---|
| Glutamate plus malate, ADP present | 42 |
| Plus rotenone | 4 |
| Plus rotenone, then succinate | 38 |
| Plus antimycin A | 3 |
| Plus cyanide | 2 |
| Plus oligomycin | 9 |
| Plus 2,4-dinitrophenol | 46 |
| Plus oligomycin, then 2,4-dinitrophenol | 44 |
stem: Rotenone lowers oxygen consumption to 4, but adding succinate restores it to 38. What does this show?

options.A: Rotenone inhibits complex II directly and succinate displaces it
options.B: Rotenone inhibits ATP synthase, and succinate bypasses the synthase
options.C: Rotenone blocks complex I, and succinate feeds electrons in at complex II
options.D: Rotenone blocks complex IV, and succinate repairs the oxidase

explanation: Rotenone inhibits the quinone-binding site of complex I, so NADH cannot be oxidized and oxygen consumption collapses. Succinate is oxidized by complex II, which donates electrons to ubiquinone downstream of the block, so respiration resumes. The restored rate is slightly lower because succinate yields FADH2, which pumps fewer protons than NADH.
memorize: Rotenone blocks complex I; succinate enters at complex II and bypasses it
Complex II contributes FADH2, so it yields less ATP than NADH

fm.formula: electron entry point determines the proton gradient and ATP yield
fm.variables: NADH enters at complex I and FADH2 at complex II; each NADH pumps 10 protons and each FADH2 pumps 6
fm.why: Bypassing complex I skips four protons of pumping, which lowers the ATP yield per pair of electrons
fm.no_calc: Succinate skips complex I, so fewer ATP per oxygen consumed

correct_rationale_plain: Rotenone blocks complex I, and succinate supplies electrons at complex II, which feeds ubiquinone downstream of the block.

wrong.A: Rotenone is a complex I inhibitor, and succinate does not displace it from complex I
wrong.B: Oligomycin, not rotenone, inhibits ATP synthase
wrong.D: Cyanide blocks complex IV; rotenone has no effect there

sc: Complex I blocked plus complex II substrate equals respiration returns.
mn: Rotenone shuts gate one; succinate uses gate two.

stem: At which complex does antimycin A act?

options.A: Complex III, blocking electron transfer from cytochrome b to cytochrome c1

explanation: Antimycin A binds the Qi site of cytochrome bc1 and prevents the Q cycle from passing electrons to cytochrome c1. Electrons cannot reach cytochrome c, so oxygen consumption falls almost to zero and no proton gradient is built. Succinate cannot rescue this block because complex II also delivers electrons through complex III.
memorize: Antimycin A blocks complex III between cytochromes b and c1
Complex III is the only route from ubiquinol to cytochrome c

fm.formula: NADH and FADH2 both reduce ubiquinone, which passes electrons through complex III
fm.variables: Complex III contains cytochrome b, the Rieske protein and cytochrome c1
fm.why: Blocking the only exit from the quinone pool stops both NADH and FADH2 oxidation, so oxygen consumption collapses
fm.no_calc: Respiration near zero despite substrate means a shared downstream block

correct_rationale_plain: Antimycin A blocks the Q cycle in complex III, cutting the shared path from both complex I and complex II to cytochrome c.

wrong.B: Rotenone blocks complex I, and succinate would restore respiration past it
wrong.C: Complex II is blocked by malonate, and antimycin A does not affect it
wrong.D: Complex IV is blocked by cyanide and carbon monoxide

sc: Antimycin equals complex III equals no route to cytochrome c.

stem: Cyanide is toxic because it binds which target?

options.B: Cytochrome c in the intermembrane space
options.D: Ferric heme a3 of cytochrome c oxidase, blocking oxygen reduction

explanation: Cyanide binds the ferric heme a3 of cytochrome c oxidase, the complex that reduces oxygen to water. With complex IV blocked, the entire chain backs up, the proton gradient collapses, and cells cannot make ATP aerobically. Oxygen consumption falls to 2, matching the table.
memorize: Cyanide, azide and carbon monoxide inhibit cytochrome c oxidase
Complex IV reduces oxygen to water and pumps two protons

fm.formula: 2 cytochrome c reduced + 0.5 O2 + 2 H+ goes to 2 cytochrome c oxidized + H2O
fm.variables: Cytochrome c oxidase contains heme a, heme a3 and copper centers
fm.why: If the terminal oxidase cannot reduce oxygen, no electron acceptor remains and the chain stops
fm.no_calc: Respiration at 5 percent of control points to the terminal oxidase

correct_rationale_plain: Cyanide binds ferric heme a3 in complex IV, so oxygen cannot be reduced and the chain halts.

wrong.A: The adenine nucleotide translocase is inhibited by atractyloside, not cyanide
wrong.B: Cytochrome c is a mobile carrier and is not the cyanide target
wrong.C: Oligomycin binds ATP synthase, not cyanide

sc: Cyanide equals complex IV equals no oxygen reduction.
mn: Cyanide: cytochrome c oxidase, cyanide chokes it.

stem: Oligomycin lowers oxygen consumption to 9 without blocking any electron carrier. What is its mechanism?

options.A: It strips the proton gradient by carrying protons across the membrane
options.B: It blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase, so the gradient builds and back-pressure slows the chain
options.C: It blocks complex I quinone binding

explanation: Oligomycin binds the F0 subunit of ATP synthase and stops proton flow through the enzyme. Protons continue to be pumped, but the gradient cannot be discharged, so the proton-motive force rises until it opposes further pumping. Respiration slows even though every electron carrier remains functional.
memorize: Oligomycin blocks ATP synthase F0 and slows respiration through back-pressure
Uncouplers release that back-pressure and raise respiration

fm.formula: proton-motive force = chemical gradient plus membrane potential
fm.variables: Pumping builds the gradient; ATP synthase discharges it; oligomycin blocks the discharge
fm.why: A large gradient increases the energy needed to pump each proton, so the chain slows to a new steady state
fm.no_calc: Respiration falls despite intact carriers, the signature of back-pressure

correct_rationale_plain: Oligomycin blocks proton flow through ATP synthase, the gradient backs up, and electron transport slows.

wrong.A: That describes an uncoupler such as dinitrophenol, which raises rather than lowers respiration
wrong.C: Complex I inhibition is rotenone, and succinate would bypass it
wrong.D: Shuttle inhibition would lower NADH supply, but oligomycin acts inside the synthase

sc: Oligomycin equals synthase block equals gradient back-pressure.

stem: 2,4-Dinitrophenol raises oxygen consumption to 46 but ATP synthesis falls. What explains both effects?

options.A: It activates ATP synthase directly, so more ATP is made per oxygen
options.B: It blocks complex IV and cells compensate by using more oxygen
options.C: It carries protons across the inner membrane, dissipating the gradient that ATP synthase needs
options.D: It increases the proton-pumping efficiency of complex I

explanation: Dinitrophenol is a lipid-soluble weak acid that shuttles protons across the inner membrane, short-circuiting the gradient. The chain runs faster because back-pressure is relieved, but the energy is released as heat instead of ATP. This is why uncouplers cause hyperthermia and weight loss despite high oxygen consumption.
memorize: Uncouplers carry protons across the membrane and separate oxidation from phosphorylation
Uncoupling raises oxygen consumption and lowers ATP output

fm.formula: ATP synthesis requires proton flow through ATP synthase, not through the lipid bilayer
fm.variables: The proton-motive force has a chemical and an electrical component; uncouplers collapse both
fm.values: oxygen consumption 42 to 46, ATP synthesis near zero
fm.substitution: 46/42 is about 1.1, a 10 percent rise in respiration
fm.why: If protons return through the bilayer instead of the synthase, the gradient cannot do work and energy becomes heat
fm.no_calc: Faster respiration with less ATP means the gradient is leaking

correct_rationale_plain: Dinitrophenol shuttles protons across the membrane, so the gradient is wasted as heat and ATP synthesis drops even as oxygen consumption rises.

wrong.A: ATP synthase is not activated, and ATP production falls
wrong.B: Complex IV is not blocked, and cyanide shows what a complex IV block looks like
wrong.D: Efficiency falls, not rises; the same electrons pump protons that then leak back

sc: Uncoupler equals protons leak equals heat, not ATP.
mn: DNP punches a hole in the dam.

stem: How many ATP are produced per oxygen atom reduced when electrons enter from NADH?
explanation: NADH donates electrons at complex I, and the chain pumps 10 protons per NADH oxidized. ATP synthase uses about four protons per ATP once the phosphate and proton transport costs are included, giving a P/O ratio of 2.5. FADH2 enters at complex II, pumps only six protons, and gives 1.5.
memorize: P/O ratio: 2.5 for NADH, 1.5 for FADH2
Ten protons pumped per NADH and six per FADH2

fm.formula: P/O = protons pumped per electron pair / protons per ATP
fm.variables: NADH pumps 10 protons; about 4 protons are needed per ATP synthesized
fm.why: The proton count sets how many turns of ATP synthase the gradient can support
fm.no_calc: Ten over four is two and a half

correct_rationale_plain: NADH pumps 10 protons, and at about 4 protons per ATP the yield is 2.5 ATP per oxygen atom.

wrong.B: 1.5 is the FADH2 value, where only six protons are pumped
wrong.C: 1.0 would require most of the gradient to be wasted
wrong.D: 4.0 is the number of protons per ATP, not the ATP yield per oxygen

mn: Two and a half for NADH, one and a half for FADH2.

stem: Why does succinate oxidation yield less ATP per oxygen atom than NADH oxidation?

options.A: Succinate produces fewer electrons per molecule
options.B: Succinate enters at complex II, so complex I proton pumping is bypassed
options.C: Succinate is oxidized in the cytosol rather than the matrix

explanation: Complex II transfers electrons from FADH2 to ubiquinone but does not pump protons, so the electrons skip the four protons normally pumped at complex I. Only complexes III and IV contribute, giving six protons and a P/O of 1.5. The electron count is the same; the entry point differs.
memorize: Complex II does not pump protons
FADH2 bypasses complex I and yields 1.5 ATP per oxygen atom

fm.variables: NADH route pumps 10 protons; FADH2 route pumps 6
fm.why: Only complexes III and IV pump when electrons enter at complex II, so the gradient is smaller per electron pair
fm.no_calc: Six over four is one and a half

correct_rationale_plain: Succinate feeds complex II, skipping complex I proton pumping, so fewer protons are available and the yield is 1.5 instead of 2.5.

wrong.A: Succinate oxidation transfers two electrons, the same as NADH
wrong.C: Succinate is oxidized on the matrix side by complex II
wrong.D: Succinate does not uncouple; the lower yield reflects a shorter proton-pumping route

sc: Entry at complex II skips four pumped protons.
mn: Complex II is a doorway, not a pump.

stem: How many protons are pumped across the inner membrane per NADH oxidized by the electron transport chain?
explanation: Complex I pumps four protons, complex III pumps four through the Q cycle, and complex IV pumps two, for a total of ten per NADH. Complex II pumps none, which is why FADH2 yields six. The resulting gradient drives ATP synthase, whose c-ring determines how many protons are needed per ATP.
memorize: Proton pumping: complex I four, complex III four, complex IV two
Complex II pumps no protons

fm.variables: Each complex contributes a fixed number of protons per electron pair
fm.why: Each pumping complex uses the energy of the electron transfer to move a defined number of protons against the gradient

correct_rationale_plain: Four protons at complex I, four at complex III and two at complex IV add up to ten per NADH.

wrong.A: Two is only complex IV, the terminal pump
wrong.B: Four is the contribution of complex I alone, or of complex III alone
wrong.C: Six is the FADH2 route, which skips complex I

sc: 4 plus 4 plus 2 equals 10; FADH2 skips the first 4.
mn: Ten for NADH, six for FADH2.

stem: ATP synthase converts the proton gradient into ATP. Which statement about the enzyme is correct?

options.A: The F1 portion spans the membrane and forms the proton channel
options.B: It pumps protons using ATP hydrolysis during normal oxidative phosphorylation
options.C: Proton flow through the F0 channel rotates the c-ring and drives ATP release from F1
options.D: It requires a sodium gradient rather than a proton gradient

explanation: F0 is the membrane-embedded rotor and channel, and F1 carries the catalytic beta subunits. Protons flowing down their gradient turn the c-ring and the gamma shaft, which forces conformational changes that bind ADP and phosphate, form ATP and release it. The enzyme can hydrolyze ATP to pump protons in reverse, but not during normal synthesis.
memorize: F0 is the proton channel and rotor; F1 contains the catalytic sites
Proton flow drives rotation and ATP release; ATP hydrolysis can reverse it

fm.formula: ADP + Pi + n H+ (outside) goes to ATP + H2O + n H+ (inside)
fm.variables: n is set by the number of c subunits in the rotor, about 8 in mammalian mitochondria
fm.values: about 4 protons per ATP including transport costs
fm.substitution: not needed; the coupling is rotational
fm.why: Rotation couples proton translocation to sequential changes in nucleotide affinity at the beta subunits

correct_rationale_plain: Protons passing through F0 rotate the c-ring and gamma shaft, and that rotation drives ATP synthesis and release at F1.

wrong.A: F1 sits on the matrix side; F0 is the membrane-spanning proton channel
wrong.B: The synthase makes ATP under oxidative conditions; reverse hydrolysis happens only when the gradient collapses
wrong.D: The mitochondrial gradient is a proton gradient, not a sodium gradient

mn: Flow spins the rotor; the rotor stamps ATP.

stem: Which citric acid cycle enzyme is the main regulated step, and what activates it?
explanation: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is allosterically activated by ADP and inhibited by ATP and NADH, so the cycle speeds up when energy charge falls. It is also activated by calcium in muscle during contraction. Citrate synthase is inhibited, not activated, by NADH and succinyl-CoA.
memorize: Isocitrate dehydrogenase: activated by ADP and calcium, inhibited by ATP and NADH
Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is inhibited by succinyl-CoA and NADH

fm.formula: cycle flux rises when ADP/ATP and NAD+/NADH ratios rise
fm.variables: Isocitrate dehydrogenase senses ADP, ATP, NADH and calcium
fm.why: ADP signals low energy charge, so activating the enzyme increases NADH production for the chain
fm.no_calc: ADP means low energy, so the cycle should speed up

correct_rationale_plain: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is activated by ADP and inhibited by ATP and NADH, making it the cycle's main control point.

wrong.B: Fumarase is not a regulated step and is not activated by ATP
wrong.C: Citrate synthase is inhibited by NADH and succinyl-CoA rather than activated
wrong.D: Malate dehydrogenase is not the main control point and is not activated by citrate

sc: Low energy means high ADP, which activates isocitrate dehydrogenase.
mn: ADP pushes the cycle; ATP and NADH put on the brakes.

stem: Which citric acid cycle reaction produces a high-energy phosphate bond directly?

options.B: Succinyl-CoA synthetase, converting succinyl-CoA to succinate and GTP

explanation: Succinyl-CoA synthetase couples cleavage of the thioester to phosphorylation of GDP or ADP, making GTP or ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation. The other cycle steps make NADH or FADH2, which yield ATP only through oxidative phosphorylation. The GTP can be converted to ATP by nucleoside diphosphate kinase.
memorize: Succinyl-CoA synthetase is the only substrate-level phosphorylation in the citric acid cycle
Succinyl-CoA to succinate yields GTP, readily converted to ATP

fm.formula: succinyl-CoA + GDP + Pi goes to succinate + GTP + CoA
fm.variables: The thioester energy is conserved in the phosphoanhydride bond of GTP
fm.values: one GTP per turn, two per glucose
fm.why: Thioester hydrolysis is coupled to nucleotide phosphorylation without a membrane gradient
fm.no_calc: One per turn, two turns per glucose

correct_rationale_plain: Succinyl-CoA synthetase makes GTP directly from succinyl-CoA, the cycle's only substrate-level phosphorylation.

wrong.A: Citrate synthase makes citrate and releases CoA, with no nucleotide phosphorylation
wrong.C: Aconitase isomerizes citrate to isocitrate without making a high-energy phosphate
wrong.D: Complex II transfers electrons to ubiquinone and makes no ATP directly

sc: Thioester cleavage plus GDP equals GTP.
mn: Succinyl-CoA: the cycle's own ATP mint.

stem: Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase requires the same cofactors as pyruvate dehydrogenase. Which set is correct?

options.D: Thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, coenzyme A, FAD and NAD+

explanation: Both enzymes are alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complexes with three catalytic subunits: a thiamine-dependent decarboxylase, a lipoate-using transacetylase, and an FAD-containing dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase that reduces NAD+. The same five cofactors are therefore required, and both produce NADH and a thioester.
memorize: Alpha-keto acid dehydrogenases need TPP, lipoate, CoA, FAD and NAD+
Thiamine deficiency impairs pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase

fm.formula: alpha-ketoglutarate + CoA + NAD+ goes to succinyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH
fm.variables: TPP decarboxylates, lipoate transfers acyl groups, CoA accepts the acyl group, FAD and NAD+ carry electrons
fm.values: five cofactors, one NADH and one CO2 per reaction
fm.why: The chemistry mirrors pyruvate dehydrogenase, so the cofactor requirements are identical

correct_rationale_plain: Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase uses TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD and NAD+, just like pyruvate dehydrogenase.

wrong.A: Biotin, ascorbate and vitamin K belong to other carboxylases and electron carriers
wrong.B: TPP alone cannot transfer the acyl group or regenerate the enzyme
wrong.C: Tetrahydrofolate and cobalamin handle one-carbon transfers, not alpha-keto acid oxidation

sc: Two alpha-keto dehydrogenases, one cofactor list.
mn: TPP, lipoate, CoA, FAD, NAD: the five-pack.

stem: Fluoroacetate is converted in cells to fluorocitrate, which inhibits aconitase. Which intermediate accumulates?
explanation: Aconitase converts citrate to isocitrate, so blocking it causes citrate to pile up behind the block. Fluorocitrate is a suicide inhibitor formed when fluoroacetate is activated to fluoroacetyl-CoA and condensed with oxaloacetate. The resulting citrate accumulation also inhibits phosphofructokinase-1, slowing glycolysis.
memorize: Fluoroacetate becomes fluorocitrate and blocks aconitase
Aconitase converts citrate to isocitrate

fm.formula: citrate goes to isocitrate via aconitase
fm.variables: Aconitase contains an iron-sulfur cluster that fluorocitrate targets
fm.values: not needed; the substrate of the blocked step accumulates
fm.why: Inhibition raises the concentration of the substrate that cannot be converted, which is citrate here
fm.no_calc: Whatever builds up is the substrate just before the block

correct_rationale_plain: Aconitase is blocked, so its substrate citrate accumulates.

wrong.A: Isocitrate is the product of aconitase and therefore falls
wrong.B: Alpha-ketoglutarate is downstream of isocitrate dehydrogenase
wrong.D: Succinate is far downstream and does not accumulate at the aconitase step

sc: Fluorocitrate blocks aconitase; citrate backs up.

stem: Why is oxygen consumption high when oligomycin and dinitrophenol are both present?

options.A: The uncoupler restores proton leak, so the gradient no longer limits electron transport even though ATP synthase is blocked
options.B: Oligomycin is displaced from ATP synthase by dinitrophenol
options.D: Oligomycin becomes an electron carrier in the presence of dinitrophenol

explanation: Oligomycin blocks the synthase, which would normally build up the gradient and slow the chain. Dinitrophenol provides an alternative proton path, so the gradient is discharged and electron transport runs at maximal uncoupled rate. ATP synthesis remains blocked because protons bypass the synthase entirely.
memorize: Uncoupler plus synthase inhibitor equals fast respiration, no ATP
Back-pressure from the gradient is what slows respiration when the synthase is blocked

fm.formula: respiration rate depends on the proton-motive force opposing pumping
fm.variables: Oligomycin blocks the synthase; dinitrophenol increases membrane proton conductance
fm.why: A leaky membrane keeps the gradient low, so proton pumping is not opposed and the chain runs near maximal rate
fm.no_calc: Fast oxygen use with no ATP means the gradient is leaking

correct_rationale_plain: Dinitrophenol lets protons leak back, relieving the back-pressure that oligomycin created, so oxygen consumption stays high while ATP synthesis stays blocked.

wrong.B: Dinitrophenol does not bind or displace oligomycin; it acts on the membrane
wrong.C: The synthase remains inhibited, which is why ATP is not made
wrong.D: Dinitrophenol is a proton carrier, not an electron carrier

sc: Oligomycin builds pressure; uncoupler releases it.
mn: Plug the turbine, open the spillway: same flow, no power.

stem: Succinate restores respiration after rotenone but not after antimycin A. What is the best explanation?

options.A: Succinate reduces complex III directly, bypassing antimycin A
options.B: Succinate donates electrons at complex II, which is upstream of the antimycin A block but downstream of complex I
options.C: Antimycin A also inhibits complex II

explanation: Complex II feeds electrons into the ubiquinone pool, which is downstream of complex I and upstream of complex III. Rotenone blocks complex I, so succinate can still supply the quinone pool and respiration resumes. Antimycin A blocks complex III, which every electron from both complexes must pass, so no substrate can rescue it.
memorize: Complex II enters the quinone pool between complex I and complex III
A block at complex III stops both NADH and FADH2 oxidation

fm.formula: electron route: NADH to complex I to Q to complex III to cytochrome c to complex IV
fm.variables: Succinate reduces complex II, which reduces Q; antimycin A blocks complex III
fm.values: 38 with succinate after rotenone, 3 with antimycin A
fm.why: Rescue is possible only if the alternate substrate enters downstream of the block and upstream of the remaining chain
fm.no_calc: Succinate enters before complex III, so only the complex III block is fatal

correct_rationale_plain: Succinate feeds the quinone pool after complex I but before complex III, so it bypasses rotenone and cannot bypass antimycin A.

wrong.A: Succinate does not reduce complex III; it reduces complex II
wrong.C: Antimycin A acts on complex III, and succinate oxidation at complex II is unaffected
wrong.D: No chemical neutralization occurs; the difference is pathway position

sc: Rescue works only if the substrate enters downstream of the block.
mn: Succinate slips in at gate two, not past gate three.

stem: Malonate slows succinate oxidation in a pattern that is reversed by raising succinate. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Malonate is an uncompetitive inhibitor of complex II
options.B: Malonate lowers Vmax of complex II without changing Km
options.C: Malonate binds cytochrome c and blocks electron transfer
options.D: Malonate is a competitive inhibitor of succinate dehydrogenase, so higher succinate restores flux

explanation: Malonate is a dicarboxylate that resembles succinate and occupies the same binding site on complex II. Because it competes reversibly, raising succinate displaces it and restores oxidation, and the apparent Km for succinate rises while Vmax is unchanged. This is the same competitive pattern seen with any structural analog.
memorize: Malonate is a competitive inhibitor of succinate dehydrogenase at complex II
Competitive inhibition is relieved by more substrate

fm.variables: Malonate competes with succinate at the complex II active site
fm.substitution: not needed; the direction is set by competition
fm.why: A competitive inhibitor raises the substrate concentration needed for half-maximal flux without lowering the maximal flux
fm.no_calc: Relief by more substrate means competition at the same site

correct_rationale_plain: Malonate competes with succinate at complex II, so extra succinate outcompetes it and restores oxidation.

wrong.A: Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only the enzyme-substrate complex and are not relieved by more substrate
wrong.B: A pure noncompetitive pattern lowers Vmax and leaves Km alone
wrong.C: Malonate acts at complex II, not at cytochrome c

sc: Analog plus relief by substrate equals competitive.
mn: Malonate mimics succinate and takes its seat.
